questions.q: A wire of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> is hanging from a fixed support. The length changes to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> when masses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> are suspended respectively from its free end. Then the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> is equal to
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
From Hooke's law, ∆L=FLAY⇒∆L∝F. Therefore,

L2-LL1-L=m2gm1g=21 ⇒L=2L1-L2

questions.q: Two wires A and B are made of same material having ratio of lengths $\frac{L_A}{L_B}=\frac{1}{3}$ and their diameters ratio $\frac{d_A}{d_B}=2$. If both the wires are stretched using same force, what would be the ratio of their respective elongations?
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
$\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{B}}}=2$
$\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}$ and $\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}$
Given, $F_A=F_B$ and $Y_A=Y_B$
$\frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}}{\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right)$
$\frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{~d}_{\mathrm{B}}^2}{\frac{\pi}{4} \mathrm{~d}_{\mathrm{A}}^2}\right)=\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right)^2$
$\frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{12}$

questions.q: The Young's modulus of a steel wire of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>6</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> and cross-sectional area <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><mo> </mo><msup><mi>mm</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mo> </mo><mo>×</mo><mo> </mo><msup><mn>11</mn><mn>11</mn></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> . The wire is suspended from its support on a given planet. A block of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> is attached to the free end of the wire. The acceleration due to gravity on the planet is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math> of its value on the earth. The elongation of wire is (Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>g</mi></math> on the earth <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>=</mo><mo> </mo><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> ):
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The external force or tension F acting on the wire is its own weight. It is given by

 F= mg=4 kg×104 m s-2=10 N

The formula to calculate the Young's modulus of the material of the wire is given by

Y= FA∆LL= FL∆LA..........................(1)

where, A is the cross-sectional area, L is the original length and ∆L is the elongation of the wire.

Substitute the given values of the known parameters into equation (1) and solve to calculate the required elongation of the wire.

2×1011 N/m2= 10 N×6 m∆L×3 mm2×1 m2106 mm2∆L= 10 N×6 m2×1011 N/m2×3 mm2×1 m2106 mm2= 0.0001 m×103 mm1 m= 0.1 mm

If the Young's modulus of wire is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>16</mn><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>11</mn></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math>, the extension of wire over its natural length is:

v=Tμ

questions.q: An aluminium rod with Young’s modulus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo> </mo><mo>×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>10</mn></msup><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math> undergoes elastic strain of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>04</mn><mo>%</mo></math>. The energy per unit volume stored in the rod in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>SI</mi></math> unit
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The data given is 

Y=7×1010 N m-2 and∆ll=0.04100

Young's modulus is given by the ratio of stress and strain,

Y=FA∆ll=FlA∆l

The energy stored is given as 

E=YA2l∆l2⇒E=YA2∆ll2×l   ...(i)

The energy per unit volume can be written from equation (i)

EV=Y2×∆ll2   ...(ii)

Substituting the values in equation (ii)

EV=12×7×1010×0.04×0.04104=56×102

A=625×10-6

Wire <math><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math> is <math><mn>2</mn><mi> </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> long and has radius <math><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo>.</mo></math> Wire <math><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></math> is <math><mn>1.5</mn><mi> </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> long and has radius <math><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal"> </mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mo>.</mo></math> If the two wires stretch by the same length for a given load, the value of <math><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></math> is close to:

questions.q: A 3 m long wire of radius 3 mm shows an extension of 0.1 mm when loaded vertically by a mass of 50 kg in an experiment to determine Young's modulus. The value of Young's modulus of the wire as per this experiment is $\mathrm{P} \times 10^{11} \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$, where the value of P is: (Take $\left.\mathrm{g}=3 \pi \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{50 \mathrm{~g}}{\pi \mathrm{r}^2}=\mathrm{y} \cdot \frac{\Delta \ell}{\ell} \\ & \frac{50 \times 3 \pi}{\pi \times\left(3 \times 10^{-3}\right)^2}=\mathrm{P} \times 10^{11} \times \frac{0.1 \times 10^{-3}}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}=\frac{50 \times 3 \times 3}{3^2 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{11} \times 0.1 \times 10^{-3}} \\ & \mathrm{P}=5\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A wire of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi></math> is clamped rigidly at one end. When the other end of the wire is pulled by a force<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo> </mo><mi>f</mi></math>, its length increases by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>l</mi></math>. Another wire of same material of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></math> and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi></math> is pulled by a force <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi>f</mi></math>. Then the increase in its length will be:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Young's modulus is same for both the wires since the material is same.

For the first wire,

Y=fLπr2l   ...(i)

For the second wire,

Y=2f(2L)4πr2l'   ...(ii)

Dividing (i) by (ii)

fLπr2l×4πr2l'4fL=1⇒l'=l

questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: Young’s modulus depends on the material not length and cross-sectional area. So Young’s modulus will remain same irrespective of the dimension of the wire.

The wire is stretched to double its length. Therefore, if the length of the wore was l, change in the length ∆l=l.

Applying Hooke's law,

Y=stressstrain=FlA∆l⇒F=YA∆ll=YA⇒F=2×1011×1×10-4=2×107 N

=2×1011×10-42l-ll

=2×107 N

The ratio of the Young's modulus of wire <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> to that of wire <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math> will be:

questions.solution:
Elongation in uniform wire under load is given by, Δl=FlSY, where S is area of cross-section.

As F is same for both wire and Δl is also same, we can write

ΔlF=lSY⇒lASAYA=lBSBYB

⇒52.5×10-5×YA=63×10-5×YB

⇒YAYB=1

questions.q: A wire of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> and radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi></math> is clamped at one end. If its other end is pulled by a force <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>F</mi></math>, its length increases by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>l</mi></math>. If the radius of the wire and the applied force both are reduced to half of their original values keeping original length constant, the increase in length will become:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the Young's modulus of the material of the wire, in the first case, can be written as

Y=Fπr2lL   ...1

From equation (1), it follows that

F=Yπr2×lL   ...2

For the second case, the Young's modulus is given by

Y=F/2πr2/4l'L   ...3

From equation (3), it follows that

F=Yl'L×2×πr24   ...4

From equations (2) and (4), it implies that

Yπr2×lL=Yl'L×2×πr24⇒l'=2l

questions.q:
One end of a metal wire is fixed to a ceiling and a load of 2 kg hangs from the other end. A similar wire is attached to the bottom of the load and another load of 1 kg hangs from this lower wire. Then the ratio of longitudinal strain of upper wire to that of the lower wire will be

questions.solution:
As we know, change in length is given by ΔL=FLAY

Therefore, strain required ΔLL=FAY

Now the ratio will be, ΔL1 L1ΔL2 L2=F1 F2=T1 T2=3010=3

questions.q:
The volume contraction of a solid copper cube of edge length 10 cm , when subjected to a hydraulic pressure of $7 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~Pa}$, would be ____ $\mathrm{mm}^3$.
(Given bulk modulus of copper $=1.4 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}$ )

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{B}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{P}}{\frac{\Delta \mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{V}}} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{V}=\frac{7 \times 10^6}{1.4 \times 10^{11}} \times\left(10 \times 10^{-2}\right)^3 \\ & \Delta \mathrm{~V}=50 \mathrm{~mm}^3\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
By energy conservation
12·YAL·x2=12mv2
0.5×109×10-6×(0.04)20.1=201000v2
∴ v2=400
v=20 m s-1

questions.q: Two slabs with square cross section of different materials $(1,2)$ with equal sides $(l)$ and thickness $\mathrm{d}_1$ and $\mathrm{d}_2$ such that $\mathrm{d}_2=2 \mathrm{~d}_1$ and $l \gt \mathrm{d}_2$. Considering lower edges of these slabs are fixed to the floor, we apply equal shearing force on the narrow faces. The angle of deformation is $\theta_2=2 \theta_1$. If the shear moduli of material 1 is $4 \times 10^9 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$, then shear moduli of material 2 is $\mathrm{x} \times 10^9 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$, where value of $x$ is ________.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Deformation angle
$\begin{aligned}
& 2 \theta_1=\theta_2 \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \frac{\sigma_1}{\eta_1}=\frac{\sigma_2}{\eta_2}
\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2\left(\frac{\mathrm{~F}}{\ell \mathrm{~d}_1 \eta_1}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\ell \mathrm{d}_2 \eta_2} \\ & \Rightarrow \eta_2=\frac{\eta_1}{4}=1 \times 10^9 \Rightarrow x=1\end{aligned}$

questions.q: In an experiment to determine the Young's modulus, steel wires of five different lengths (1,2,3,4 and 5) but of same cross-section 2 mm2 were taken and curves between extension and load were obtained. The slope (extension/load) of the curves were plotted with the wire length and the following graph is obtained. If the Young's modulus of given steel wires is x×1011N m-2, then the value of x is _____ .
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
We know that, Young's modulus is Y=FLA∆L, where, F is force or load acting on wire, A is cross-section area, L is length and ∆L is extension in length.

Now, from given graph, the slope of the line is =ΔLWL=ΔLLW=1YA

⇒Y=1slopeA

Thus, Young's modulus of the steel wires is Y=12×10-60.25×10-5

⇒Y=2×1011 N m-2.

Therefore, x=2.
